khunia-dighi-memorial.desc: Khunia Dighi is a big pond of about six acres in Ranisankail upazila. In 1971 the Pakistani army and local collaborators brought prisoners from their Ranisankail camp here, tortured and shot them, and threw the bodies into the water. Around a thousand people are believed to have been killed, and it is the largest mass-killing site in the district. A memorial now stands on the bank. It is a sombre, quiet place to understand what the war meant in this corner of the country.
blocks: How to get there
From Ranisankail upazila town (bus from Thakurgaon), it is a short auto ride to Khunia Dighi in Hosengaon union.
Good to know
Behave as you would at a graveyard. Combine with Raja Tonkonath's palace in the same upazila.

jamalpur-zamindar-bari-mosque.desc: The Jamalpur zamindar family laid the foundation of their house in 1862, and work on the mosque beside it began in 1867. What makes it stand out is the roof: around 28 slender minarets, each roughly 35 feet tall and patterned differently, rise around three decorated domes. The walls inside and out are covered with floral and creeper motifs, and a big ornamental gateway leads into the compound. It is a protected monument of the Department of Archaeology and still used for daily prayers.
blocks: How to get there
From Thakurgaon town (about 8 km), take an auto on the Pirganj road past the airport to Shibganj Hat, then about 3 km west to Jamalpur.
Good to know
Dress modestly and avoid prayer times. Late-afternoon light shows off the minarets well.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
dholarhat-temple.desc: At Dholarhat, about 9 km north of Thakurgaon town, stand three old temples. The main one is an unusual tall, round, single-chamber shrine raised high with a stair leading up to it. Traces of decoration on its walls show it was once richly finished, and an old image is kept inside. It is one of only two sites in Thakurgaon listed by the Department of Archaeology, yet few outsiders come to see it.
blocks: How to get there
From Thakurgaon town take an auto or easy-bike north to Dholarhat (about 9 km).
Good to know
Ask at Dholarhat bazar for the 'purono mondir'. Respect worshippers if a puja is on.

nekmarad-mela.desc: The Nekmarad fair grows up each year around the shrine of the saint Pir Nekmarad in Ranisankail upazila. It has been held for centuries and was historically famous as a great livestock market, with traders bringing cattle, horses and other animals from far away. Today it also has stalls of household goods, wooden furniture, sweets and entertainment. It remains a major annual event for the district's villages.
blocks: How to get there
From Thakurgaon go to Ranisankail by bus, then take a local auto-rickshaw to Nekmarad.
Good to know
Confirm the dates locally; crowds are heavy.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
balia-mosque.desc: The Balia Mosque was built around 1910 by a local landowner, Meher Bakhsh Chowdhury, in a late Mughal style of brick and lime. For decades it stood without its domes, and local folklore said jinns had built it overnight and left before finishing. Restoration from the 2000s completed the domes and repaired the fine brickwork. It is now a well-kept, photogenic building in a village setting.
blocks: How to get there
In Choto Balia village near Bhulli, Thakurgaon Sadar; take a bus or CNG to Bhulli bazar, then a rickshaw or van.
Good to know
It is an active mosque; dress modestly and avoid prayer times.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
Small fee charged by the owners (approx.)
baliadangi-giant-mango-tree.desc: In a village of Baliadangi upazila near the border stands a mango tree said to be around two centuries old. Its massive branches have bent down to the ground and rooted again, so the tree spreads in every direction, covering a large plot. Walking beneath it feels like entering a green hall. It is often described as one of the largest mango trees in Asia, and the owners charge a small fee to visit.
blocks: How to get there
From Thakurgaon take a bus to Baliadangi, then an auto-rickshaw to the village of Harinmari.
Good to know
Visit in summer to see it laden with fruit. Do not climb or break branches.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
raja-tonkonath-palace.desc: Tonkonath Chowdhury, son of a temple priest who inherited a zamindari, built up the Malduar estate in the early 20th century and was honoured by the British and later given the title of raja. The estate was renamed Ranisankail after his wife, Rani Shankari Devi. Before Partition the family left for India, and the palace has been decaying ever since. Even half-ruined, its facades and rooms hint at how grand it once was, and it remains one of Thakurgaon's best-known sights.
blocks: How to get there
From Thakurgaon take a bus to Ranisankail (about 40 km), then an auto to the rajbari in Bachor union, beside the old Union Parishad building.
Good to know
Parts of the structure are unsafe; don't climb on walls or upper floors. Khunia Dighi memorial is in the same upazila.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
ramrai-dighi.desc: Ramrai Dighi covers more than 40 acres and is thought to date back several centuries, though its exact history is uncertain. Its high banks are planted with hundreds of litchi trees and other shade trees, making it a pleasant walk. In winter, migratory birds rest on the water. Local families come for picnics on holidays.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus from Thakurgaon to Ranisankail upazila (about an hour), then a rickshaw to the dighi.
Good to know
Visit in early summer to see the litchis ripening on the banks.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
lokayan-museum-akcha.desc: The NGO ESDO started this museum in 2006 at East Akcha village, about 4 km north of Thakurgaon town, to keep the everyday life of working rural people on record. The folk gallery has ploughs, dheki husking pedals, a palanquin, a bullock cart, coins, jewellery, pottery and wedding things. Another gallery covers the Santal, Oraon and other plains ethnic groups. The river gallery holds bottled water from about 200 Bangladeshi rivers, some of them now dead, and the Liberation War gallery keeps soil from killing fields across the country.
blocks: How to get there
Auto or easy-bike from Thakurgaon town to East Akcha, about 4 km north.
Good to know
Call ahead or check locally for opening hours, since it is a privately run museum. Good for children who have never seen a dheki or bullock cart.

thakurgaon-winter-pitha.desc: Winter comes early and sharp in Thakurgaon, and with it the pitha season. Roadside stalls make bhapa pitha, steamed rice-flour cakes filled with gur and coconut, and chitoi pitha, small clay-pan cakes eaten with spicy bhorta or molasses. New-harvest rice gives them their best flavour. The district also holds pitha festivals where home cooks show off many more varieties.
blocks: Good to know
Eat them fresh and hot; chitoi with shutki bhorta is a local favourite.

surjapuri-mango.desc: Surjapuri is a traditional variety of the far north-west, smaller than the famous Rajshahi mangoes but strongly scented and sweet. It ripens a little later than southern varieties, extending the mango season. The fruit from the giant Baliadangi tree is of this variety. Local markets sell it in heaps during the season.
blocks: Good to know
Choose fruit with a strong smell at the stem end.

glance: 405 km to Thakurgaon by road, 10–13 hours by bus or car
haripur-rajbari.desc: Haripur Rajbari was the home of a local zamindar family during the British period. The two-storey building has arched windows, decorative plasterwork and inner courtyards, now weathered and partly overgrown. It gives a sense of how landed families lived in this distant corner of Bengal. The surrounding upazila is rural and quiet, close to the Indian border.
blocks: How to get there
Buses run from Thakurgaon to Haripur via Ranisankail; ask locally for the Rajbari.
Good to know
The building is fragile; do not climb on walls. Carry ID near the border.
